analysis.one_liner: Bans BPA in food and beverage containers and forces safety re-review of food packaging chemicals.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote: it sat in the Senate health committee for the six months left in the Congress and died there.
analysis.plain_summary: This bill would have banned bisphenol A (BPA), a chemical used in food and drink containers — most famously the linings of canned food — after a short transition, treating any food sold in a BPA container as unsafe. Facilities that truly could not replace BPA could get a one-year renewable waiver, but their products would carry a prominent warning label. It also barred swapping BPA for other chemicals known to cause cancer, reproductive harm, or hormone disruption, and required the FDA to periodically re-review chemicals already approved for food packaging, including accounting for low-dose effects and vulnerable groups like infants and pregnant women.
analysis.who_benefits: Consumers — especially pregnant women, infants, and children — who would get BPA out of their food packaging or at least a clear warning label on any waiver product, plus workers and fenceline communities listed in the bill's vulnerable-population definition. Shoppers would also benefit from a system that stops the FDA from accepting a manufacturer's own safety paperwork without checking low-dose and reproductive risks.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Families eating canned and packaged food

how_it_helps.text: Treats food in containers containing or releasing BPA as adulterated — the same legal category as food contaminated with a poisonous substance — making it unlawful to sell 180 days after enactment [S3].

Lets a facility get only a one-year renewable waiver, and only by proving BPA replacement is technologically infeasible and filing a phase-out plan; waived products must carry a label warning that BPA 'can leach into food and may harm prenatal development and the health of children and adults' [S2] [S3].

Bars replacing BPA with known or likely carcinogens, EPA-listed persistent toxic chemicals, reproductive or developmental toxicants, or endocrine-disrupting chemicals, and requires promoting safer alternatives [S2] [S3].

Requires the FDA to review already-approved food packaging substances at least once every three years, factoring in low-dose exposure and vulnerable populations, and to strip approvals from substances that fail the safety determination [S2] [S3].

Closes a self-certification loophole: manufacturers and suppliers of food contact substances must notify the government of low-dose and reproductive-toxicity test results before the substance enters interstate commerce, changing 'may' to 'shall' [S3].
Preserves the right of states, localities, and tribes to set stricter rules or require their own BPA warnings, so the federal floor does not override tougher state laws [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Food and beverage canners and packaging manufacturers would bear the cost of reformulating containers and linings, and chemical companies that make BPA would lose that market. Consumers could face slightly higher packaging costs in the short run, and some waiver products would carry warning labels.
analysis.who_pays_short: Canners, packaging makers, BPA chemical producers

drawbacks.text: Reformulating containers is not free: canned-food makers and packaging manufacturers would pay retooling and reformulation costs, some of which could show up in consumer prices, and the bill gave only 180 days for most containers to comply [S3].

The waiver process depends on FDA judgment calls about what counts as 'technologically feasible' replacement, which could mean years of BPA-labeled products staying on shelves for hard-to-replace uses — the warning label informs but does not remove the exposure [S3].

Supporters would have to concede the science on low-dose BPA effects was still debated at the federal level: the FDA had declined to ban BPA when pressed in prior proceedings, so the bill effectively ordered a stricter risk judgment than the agency's own standing position, which opponents called premature.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The core trade is real but one-sided in the evidence: BPA can leach from can linings into food, and the bill's own label language ties it to prenatal and child-health harm, while replacement linings already existed for many products. The waiver-and-warning structure handles the genuinely hard cases. The main honest criticism is timing and cost: a fast compliance deadline imposed reformulation costs on an entire industry, and a safety re-review mandate would have added workload to an under-resourced FDA.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced and sent to the Senate health committee, which never acted on it, and the bill died when the two-year Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Edward Markey introduced the Ban Poisonous Additives Act of 2014 on July 9, 2014, and it was read twice and referred to the Committee on Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions [S1] [S5].
That referral was the bill's only action: the HELP Committee never held a hearing or a markup, and the full Senate never voted on it [S5].
The bill drew just one cosponsor in its roughly six months of life, and the 113th Congress ended on January 3, 2015, killing the bill [S1] [S4] [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Canned-food and beverage companies, packaging manufacturers, and BPA producers are better off: they never had to reformulate containers, absorb the compliance costs, or put warning labels on any of their products. Shoppers who want BPA-free packaging gained nothing beyond what the market was already voluntarily doing.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Canners and packaging makers kept the status quo

for.name: Sen. Edward Markey
for.what_they_did: Sponsored the bill to ban BPA in food containers and require FDA re-review of packaging chemicals

against.name: Senate HELP Committee
against.role: Committee the bill was referred to
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled a hearing or markup; the bill sat in committee from July 2014 until the Congress ended

sides.party_line_note: With only two Democratic sponsors and no votes or committee action ever taken, the record shows a two-senator Democratic bill that died quietly rather than a partisan floor fight.

industries.industry: Food and beverage canners and packaging makers
industries.note: BPA-based epoxy linings are the standard for canned food and drink, so the ban would have forced reformulation within 180 days for most containers, with waiver products carrying a health warning on the label. Continuing to sell food in BPA-lined cans avoids those costs while leaving consumers exposed to the chemical the bill's label language links to prenatal and child health harm.

The bill eliminates the BPA market in food packaging and subjects replacement chemicals to restrictions on carcinogens, endocrine disruptors, and reproductive toxicants, plus mandatory FDA re-review of already-approved packaging substances — closing the self-certification channel that lets a manufacturer's own safety paperwork clear a substance for commerce.
The bill directs HHS to promote, facilitate, and incentivize safer alternatives, creating demand for BPA-free containers and replacement linings that meet the bill's safety criteria.
